searchText: I'll ask here instead of the BLS precompile thread as there are more cryptographers that look here. The issue is the following - the algorithm to perform a linear combination in BLS is sublinear in the number of points - problem is that we perform the subgroup check on each of the points in the input. Since this check is O(1) for each point, the check itself is linear in the number of points. - this makes the whole linear combination take linear time in the input. - I claim that if instead of doing the check point by point we do (possibly multiple) random linear combinations of the same input points and check the sum is in the subgroup then we keep the sublinear structure of the algorithm and it's safe anyway, since each such random combination would give approx 1/h probability of certainty where h is the index of the subgroup. Is the above standard or not? Cause it seems straightforward A nit pick: generating N random scalars is also O(N). I'll ask here instead of the BLS precompile thread as there are more cryptographers that look here. The issue is the following
- the algorithm to perform a linear combination in BLS is sublinear in the number of points
- problem is that we perform the subgroup check on each of the points in the input. Since this check is O(1) for each point, the check itself is linear in the number of points. 
- this makes the whole linear combination take linear time in the input. 
- I claim that if instead of doing the check point by point we do (possibly multiple) random linear combinations of the same input points and check the sum is in the subgroup then we keep the sublinear structure of the algorithm and it's safe anyway, since each such random combination would give approx 1/h probability of certainty where h is the index of the subgroup.

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
I think this is not secure because the probability of an element passing the check that is not in the subgroup is 1/size_of_subgroup.

If we imagine there is a point P in the prime order subgroup, ie the check should pass for P. 

Then we imagine that there is a point of order 2 called B. The check should fail when given B, or P + B.

I will now check B and P+B.

We generate two random elements r1, r2 and the sum S = r1 * B + r2 * (P+B)

If r1 and r2 are even then the check passes since B has order 2. The probability of r1 and r2 being even is (1/2)^2
